full_judgment:
Kemaluddin Hossain, J.-This appeal raises a complex question of interpretation of Section 20(5)(c)(ii) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act 1950. The facts are that the plaintiff-respondents instituted a title suit for declaration of title and for khas possession of the suit lands after evicting the defendants therefrom and further for declaring the decision by the Revenue Officer dated 23.12.54 in Misc. Case No. 2 of the R.O.S. Court Barisal a nullity Their case in short in that Kemaluddin Sardar predecessor of the plaintiffs created a Wakf of the suit property by a Wahfnama of 28.12.1891. The plaintiff No. 1 is managing the Wakf property as Mutwalli of the Wakf estate. In terms of the Wakfnama the plaintiffs as the heirs of three sons of Kemaluddin Sardar are entitled to enjoy the usufruct of the wakf property after meeting expenses for charitable, religious and other purposes, Thus leaving aside the land for the expenses for charitable purposes, the balance of the Wakf properties are to be divided into three parts representing the heirs of the three .sons of Kemaluddin Sardar. It is alleged that there was a proceeding before the Revenue Officer; Barisal who directed acquisition of Schedule 'Kha' properties which were found to be in excess under the provisions of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act 1950. The Revenue Officer treated the all Wakf properties as one unit belonging to one family instead of treating the properties belonging to three families of the heirs of three sons of the Wakf. 

 4. The scheme of section 20 may be looked at. The section contemplates the sequel to the acquisition of all rent-receiving interests." The section covers the holders of all categories of land, not only the rent-receiver but cultivating riyat, cultivating under raiyat and non-agricultural tenant. The section also defines the quality and quantity of the land each of them can hold. Sub-section (1) of section 20 days that on the acquisition of all rent-receiving interests, no rent-receiver, agricultural or non-agricultural tenant shall be entitled to retain possession of any of his khas lands in such area except as provided in the suit-section (2). This sub-section divides all khas lands into retainable and non-retainable. Retainable khas land is again subject to quantitative ceiling fixed by it. 

 The sub-section says, a person allowed to retain khas land shall be entitled to retain as tenant under the (Provincial) Government, homestead, land used for agricultural or horticultural purposes including tanks, land cultivable or capable of cultivation on reclamation and vacant non-agricultural lands. These are retainable khas land: Any land or building in a hat or bazar, fishery, forest and ferry are excluded from the category of retainable khas lands they are non-retainable khas land. The sub-section fixes a quantitative ceiling to the retainable khas land. While fixing the quantity the measure is the holder of the land and the members of his family. It says, any one of the allowable person shall be entitled to retain 100 standard beghas or ten standard beghas for each member of the family, whichever is greater. An explanation has been appended describing the family. According to the explanation 'family' shall mean any person under sub-section (1) and .all persons leaving in the same mess and dependent upon him but does, not include any servant or hired labourer. 

 6.Clause (c) does not pose any complication. All wakf which are exclusively for religious or charitable purposes will be allowed to retain all retainable khas land. But complexity arises with clause C(ii). It says among others that any wakf-al-aulad the income from the land covered by such wakf is partly dedicated for religious or charitable purposes, and partly for pecuniary benefit of any individual, only such portion of the land, as may be selected in accordance with the rules framed by the Government, shall come within the purview of the retainable khas land of the wakf. This clause is silent how the land is covered by charitable or religious purposes but meant for pecuniary benefit of any individual is to be dealt with. The silence indicates that such land will be governed by the genus I provision of S. 20. It will be subject to the quantitative limitation set by sub-section (2). 

 9. If we now revert to clause C(ii) of the Act, we find the legislature has divided the corpus and not the wakf into two, Charitable and non-charitable, where the pecuniary benefit is for any individual. The Charitable part shall continue under the original wakf deed in all retainable khas land. The non-charitable part of the wakf property will be subject to the quantitative ceiling fixed by sub-section (2) for the retainable khas land. The land in excess of quantitative ceiling, no doubt, will stand acquired to the Government but the wakf estate shall get compensation for it. This part of corpus of the wakf estate is altered from land into cash money. This money is wakf. The Mutwalli, under the doctrine of cypres is bound to invest it in such other property as would yield income equal as nearly as possible to the original wakf deed. Interpreted in the way we do, there is neither bifurcation of wakf, nor its destruction nor conversion of a part of wakf property into secular property. 

 13. It is further to be remembered that the heirs of the wakf come to represent the wakf estate in their representative capacity and not in their personal capacity. The land so allotted will ensure to the benefit of the wakf estate It will subsist as part of retainable khas land of the wakf estate. Mutwalli will in his managerial capacity administer the land as" part and parcel of the wakf estate. 

 14. In our opinion any wakf al-al-aulad which is dedicated party for charitable purpose and partly for individual benefit or wholly for benefit of any individual the khas land of such wakf-al-al-aulad estate should be retained on the footing of the living heirs representation the wakf state on the date the section came into operation. The heirs of the wakf in the aggregate will represent the wakf estate in their representative capacity but not in their personal capacity. Calculated on this basis, the wakf-al-al-aulad estate will retain as much as it will be possible to retain above 100 beghas by as many number as the heirs will be in existence above ten. 

 18. In Khawaja Maynuddin, another Division Bench of the Dacca High Court held that on the acquisition of rent-receiving interest of Wakf estate, there is no authority in the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act for the distribution of the khas land among the beneficiaries. 

 19. We now turn to the contention of Mr. Pal. He refers to sections 3(i), 3(4)(e) and 20(5)(c)(ii), and says that the total effect of these provisions is that the law first acquires all rent receiving interests, makes all persons statutory tenants of the Government for retainable khas land, and then for the retainable khas land bifurcates the wakf into charitable and non-charitable one and by implication converts the non-charitable part into a secular estate and so the beneficiaries are entitled to allotment of this secular land in their individual capacity. He, in short, adopts the conclusion of the High Court. We have already held against this contention with reasons. In addition to those reasons it may be added that Mr. Pal's contention that the secular part of the wakf estate will go to the beneficiaries suffers from inherent contradiction. If he concedes that part of the wakf estate has become secular, then the secular part will be treated as secular property of the wakf and in that event the heirs of the wakf and not the beneficiaries of the wakf will get the land. In the present case the beneficiaries do not include the heirs of the daughters of the wakf. Mr. Pal's contention does not stand. 

 20. We now turn to the merits of the appeal. It is not disputed that the wakf of late Kemaluddin Sardar is a mixed wakf, partly dedicated to the charitable purposes and partly dedicated to the individual benefit of some of the heirs of wakf. The total khas land of the wakf estate is 72.20 acres Upon calculation the Revenue Officer found that 17'65 acres of land is required for the maintenance of charitable purposes. It is not in dispute. The dispute is now the balance of 54.55 acres of land is to be allotted. The Revenue Officer and the Trial Court allotted the land treating Mutwalli as the rent-receiver. The High Court has set aside the finding of the trial court holding this land as secular and the beneficiaries entitled to its allotment. None of the decisions is correct. According to our judgment, the heirs of the wakf will represent 4he wakf estate and land will be allotted to the wakf estate on that basis. The land so allotted will be khas land of the wakf estate. If sortie land in excess is left over on calculation, it will vest in the Government, but the compensation money for the excess land will be wakf, and the Mutwalli will be found to reinvest the same in any other suitable property. In this view of the matter, we set aside the decisions of the courts below and send the case back on remand to the Trial Court to dispose of the suit in the light of the observations made above. He will be at liberty to take such additional evidence as may be required for the disposal of the suit over and above the evidence already on record.
